6uzf: By the end of this week you can tell the story of a change of life: what you got used to, what you realised, what you dream of, and whether you became, turned into or changed into a different person.
1r3wacz: This week you review two classes that help each other a lot. The first is about verbs that always take the same preposition: if you change the preposition, the sentence sounds wrong or changes its meaning. The second is about the verbs that express, in Spanish, the idea of “changing and becoming something else”. Your guide is Carmen, an engineer from Quito who moved to Cuenca ten years ago and now weaves toquilla straw hats.
wr65oq: Some verbs always take the same preposition before a noun or an infinitive. The most practical thing is to learn them as a block, like a single word: “acostumbrarse a”, “tratar de”, “pensar en”, “soñar con”. If you change the preposition, the listener notices the mistake straight away.
thsfyo: Grouping them by preposition helps you remember them. With “a” there are usually verbs of starting or daring (aprender a, atreverse a, negarse a). With “de” there are many verbs of memory and emotions (acordarse de, olvidarse de, quejarse de). With “en”, verbs of the mind and trust (pensar en, confiar en, fijarse en). With “con”, verbs of desire and company (soñar con, contar con, casarse con).
1x5r17f: The preposition doesn’t disappear: before “que” and in questions
1dkso43: When a clause with “que” follows the verb, the preposition stays: “Me di cuenta de que el taller era pequeño”, “Confío en que lo terminemos a tiempo”. Dropping it is a frequent mistake (queísmo). The opposite mistake is adding “de” where it isn’t needed (dequeísmo): “Pienso que…”, not “Pienso de que…”. A trick: replace the clause with “eso”. If you say “me di cuenta de eso”, you need “de que”; if you say “pienso eso”, just “que”.
1v3lkhq: In questions, the preposition goes first: “¿En qué piensas?”, “¿Con quién cuentas?”, “¿De qué te quejas?”. And watch out with “pensar”: “pensar en” is to have someone or something in your mind; “¿qué piensas de…?” asks for an opinion; “pensar + infinitive” is to intend.
1sx8szt: Before writing “de que”, test it with “eso”: if the sentence needs “de eso”, keep the preposition; if not, remove it.

11r4ji1: In Spanish there isn’t a single verb for “to change and become”. “Hacerse” + adjective or noun without an article tells a change that depends on a decision or a long process: profession, beliefs, ideas, age, money (“Se hizo artesana”, “Se hizo vegetariano”, “Nos hacemos mayores”).
suujlc: “Volverse” + adjective tells a change of character or personality that the person doesn’t fully control: “Con los años se volvió más paciente”. “Convertirse en” + noun tells a complete transformation of people, things or places: “La casa de mi abuelo se convirtió en un taller”. Notice: “convertirse” always takes “en”, and “volverse” never does.
fbfxc5: Three verbs, three kinds of change
5lzxx2: “Volverse” doesn’t take “en”; with a noun, it takes “un” or “una”.
p6vlvi: Llegar a ser, pasar a ser, and volverse versus volver a
1trqdyb: “Llegar a ser” tells the goal of a long road, almost always with effort: “Llegó a ser la mejor tejedora del barrio”. “Pasar a ser” is more neutral: a change of category, post or status, frequent in the news (“El pueblo pasó a ser parte del municipio”).
lq9zto: Don’t confuse “volverse” with “volver a”, which you reviewed in week 11. “Se volvió desconfiado” is a change of character; “volvió a confiar” means he trusted again; and “volvió serio” means he came back from somewhere looking serious.

624l2o: The preposition that hides when you link words: “me acostumbré‿a”, “pienso‿en‿ti”
2o0f4w: Many of this week’s prepositions are a single vowel or start with a vowel: “a”, “en”. In speech they join the word before and the word after, and almost disappear: “me acostumbré‿a‿esto” sounds like a single word. That is why many students don’t hear them and then don’t write them.
ozrdrb: So as not to lose them, pronounce the link without a pause but without deleting the vowel: “pienso‿en‿ella”, “se convirtió‿en‿un taller”, “me atreví‿a‿hablar”. When two identical vowels meet (“voy‿a‿aprender”), lengthen the sound a little instead of saying it twice.
3ioi6f: Even if the preposition is barely heard in speech, it always appears in writing: “me acostumbré a”, “pienso en”, “se convirtió en”. Remember the contractions too: “a + el = al”, “de + el = del”.

1409pav: Thank you for having me, Carmen. I was told you were an engineer before you took this up. Is that true?
1pxmii4: Yes, I worked for twelve years at a construction company in Quito. I earned well, but one day I realised I didn’t think about anything but work. I had become a very nervous person.
d7xwnp: And why did you choose hats, of all things?
g9dxqn: Because of my grandmother. She used to weave here in Cuenca and I had dreamed of learning since I was a child. So I dared to leave my permanent job and came here with a suitcase and a lot of fears.
1lxcw06: Was it hard for you to get used to life here?
j55k37: At first, yes. It took me almost two years to weave a hat that could be sold. I complained about everything: the cold, my tired hands… But I had the help of doña Rosa, a master weaver from the neighbourhood, who was very patient with me.

vwzy0c: Yes, my grandmother’s house became the headquarters of a small cooperative. I don’t know if I’ll ever be as good as she was, but I’ve become a real craftswoman. And I’ve become much calmer, that’s for sure.

1b3rkqc: An Ecuadorian travel magazine publishes every month the profile of a person who changed their life. This month it’s Carmen’s turn.
157oypi: Ten years ago, Carmen Ordóñez calculated the strength of bridges in an office in Quito. Today she spends eight hours a day sitting by a window in the San Sebastián neighbourhood, in Cuenca, weaving toquilla straw hats. “People think I went mad,” she says, laughing. “I think I became more sensible.”
flhzca: The change was not sudden. Carmen remembers the exact afternoon she decided: she was stuck in a traffic jam, thinking about a report, and she realised she had gone months without thinking about anything else. That weekend she travelled to Cuenca, visited her grandmother’s empty house and dared to ask a question she had never asked herself: what if I stay?
1efdo22: Getting used to her new life was hard. She had to learn to work with her hands, to earn a living with much less money and to trust a master who only spoke to her when she made a mistake. For months she complained of pain in her fingers. But little by little she became a craftswoman, and her grandmother’s house became a workshop open to visitors.
8l0d0m: Today she has four apprentices and dreams of a weaving school for young people in the neighbourhood. Will she become one of Cuenca’s great masters? “That doesn’t depend on me,” she answers. “I just try to weave each hat better than the last one.”
